Unless the x86 pass is merely exposing an older combine weakness, the best fix location is more likely in that pass's profitability or placement logic than in this broad generic combiner routine.

behavior_items: The provided 'reproducer' does not contain source code; it repeats the bug report text, so the exercised program logic must be inferred from the regression description rather than from a concrete test case.

The regression is performance-only, not described as a wrong-code or crash issue. The failing condition is a 24-40% slowdown in a SPEC workload when compiled with `-Ofast -march=native -flto`, which means the reproducer primarily stresses late optimization quality and target-specific code generation on x86, especially for AMD Zen2 and Zen5.

The bisection points to commit `aba3b9d3a48a0703fd565f7c5f0caf604f59970b`, which extends the x86 `remove_redundant_vector` pass. That pass is intended to identify multiple equivalent vector values and replace them with a single shared producer, reducing redundant vector instructions.

According to the commit message, the new logic specifically handles vector broadcasts originating from constants, function arguments, and variables with a single definition. The optimization attempts to create one 'widest' broadcast and reuse it for all narrower vector uses, rather than emitting multiple broadcasts near each use site.

For constants and function arguments, the pass may hoist the widest broadcast to the entry of the nearest common dominator of all uses. The compiler behavior exercised here is therefore dominator-based code motion: moving a vector-broadcast instruction earlier in the control-flow graph because the scalar source is assumed invariant.

For single-definition variables, the pass may replace the original defining operation with a widest broadcast. This changes where and how the vector value is materialized, and can alter register pressure, live ranges, and the availability of other combines or scheduling opportunities.

A benchmark such as `lbm_r`/`cam4_r` is likely rich in loops, repeated scalar-to-vector splats, and hot vectorized kernels. In that setting, sharing one hoisted widest broadcast can be counterproductive if it lengthens the lifetime of a wide vector register across hot regions or across multiple basic blocks.

On AMD Zen2/Zen5, the slowdown suggests the transformed code interacts badly with microarchitectural costs such as register pressure, spills/reloads, instruction scheduling, port pressure, or domain/cross-lane costs of wider vector operations. Even if the instruction count drops, execution time can worsen if the hoisted broadcast becomes a long-lived value or blocks more favorable local code generation.

Because the regression appears only after this pass extension, the reproducer is effectively exercising a profitability bug in the optimization heuristic: the pass assumes that eliminating redundant broadcasts is always beneficial, but in some hot code it is better to keep broadcasts local and narrower.

The use of `-flto` matters because link-time optimization increases whole-program visibility and may expose more function arguments/constants to this pass, or enable broader CFG reshaping and vector-use merging, making the problematic hoisting/reuse decision trigger more often.

The use of `-march=native` is also important because it lets GCC select the widest available vector ISA and tune decisions for the host CPU. The phrase 'widest broadcast' implies the pass may prefer a larger vector mode than what was originally used at individual sites, which can amplify register and scheduling costs on real hardware.

The reproducer therefore exercises the interaction between target-specific vector cleanup (`remove_redundant_vector`), dominance-based placement of broadcasts, vector-width selection, and backend performance on AMD x86 cores. The failure mode is that an optimization meant to remove redundant vector setup work instead degrades runtime in a benchmark-sensitive hot path.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: This reproducer is not a source-level correctness test but a compiler-performance regression tied to GCC bug 120941. The only material provided is the bug report, which indicates that after commit `aba3b9d3a48a0703fd565f7c5f0caf604f59970b`, the x86 `remove_redundant_vector` pass began hoisting and consolidating scalar-to-vector broadcasts more aggressively. The workload compiled with `-Ofast -march=native -flto` appears to contain hot vectorized code where repeated broadcasts from constants, arguments, or single-def variables occur across multiple blocks. GCC now tries to replace those with one widest broadcast placed at a common dominator or at the scalar definition. Although semantically valid, this changes placement and width of vector materialization, likely increasing live ranges and register pressure and possibly forcing less favorable scheduling or spilling on AMD Zen2/Zen5. So the reproducer exercises a missed-profitability problem in target-specific vector optimization: fewer broadcast instructions in the IR/RTL, but worse generated machine code performance.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The common pattern is a target-specific performance regression introduced exactly by commit `aba3b9d3a48a0703fd565f7c5f0caf604f59970b`, which expanded the x86 `remove_redundant_vector` pass. The failure is not wrong-code but a large runtime slowdown under `-Ofast -march=native -flto`, so the likely bug class is a profitability/modeling defect in an optimization that changes vector broadcast placement and width. The new transformation unifies several scalar-to-vector splats into one shared 'widest' broadcast, either hoisted to a nearest common dominator for constants/function arguments or substituted at the single definition site for variables. Across the reported workloads, the shared pattern is that this can increase live ranges of wide vector registers across hot loops and multiple basic blocks, which is exactly the sort of change that can worsen register pressure, spilling, scheduling freedom, and microarchitectural throughput on AMD Zen2/Zen5. Another repeated pattern is width inflation: replacing several narrower local broadcasts with one wider broadcast may reduce static instruction count while increasing cross-lane cost, consuming scarcer wide-vector resources, or preventing later combines that relied on local materialization. The fact that `-flto` amplifies the issue suggests the pass may become more aggressive when more uses are visible, indicating weak profitability gating or insufficient target-cost feedback. Overall, the most plausible compiler bug is that the extended redundancy-removal logic assumes semantic redundancy implies performance benefit, but it fails to account for placement-sensitive and width-sensitive costs in hot x86 vector code.
possible_causes: A profitability bug in `remove_redundant_vector` hoists broadcasts to a common dominator even when doing so lengthens the live range of a wide vector across hot regions, causing extra register pressure and spills on Zen2/Zen5.

The pass may incorrectly prefer the single widest vector mode for reuse, replacing narrower per-use broadcasts with a wider splat whose execution and register-allocation cost is higher on the target microarchitecture.

The transformation for constants and function arguments likely lacks target-specific cost checks for dominator hoisting, so it removes redundant instructions in IR terms but produces worse scheduling/port-pressure behavior in machine code.

The single-definition-variable case may rewrite the defining operation too early or too broadly, preventing later local combines, rematerialization, or loop-local placement that would otherwise generate better code.

The pass may ignore hotness/loop structure when merging broadcasts across multiple blocks, moving work out of its locally optimal position and increasing the lifetime of vector temporaries through loops or across loop preheaders.

There may be a missing x86 backend heuristic or cost-model hook for AMD CPUs, so the pass treats wide broadcasts as uniformly cheap even when Zen2/Zen5 suffer more from widened vector lifetimes, spills, or cross-lane operations.

LTO-exposed whole-program visibility may let the pass merge more uses than is profitable, indicating a defect in scaling the optimization with use count, CFG span, or dominance distance rather than limiting it to clearly beneficial cases.
evidence: The regression is bisected to commit `aba3b9d3a48a0703fd565f7c5f0caf604f59970b`, whose stated purpose is to extend x86 `remove_redundant_vector` handling of broadcasts from constants, arguments, and single-def variables.

The observed failure is purely performance-related: a 24-40% slowdown rather than a crash or miscompile, which strongly points to an optimization profitability defect rather than semantic incorrectness.

The commit explicitly introduces two risky transformations: hoisting a widest broadcast to the nearest common dominator and replacing a scalar's single definition with a widest broadcast, both of which naturally change live ranges and register pressure.

The benchmark is compiled with `-Ofast -march=native -flto`, a configuration that maximizes vectorization and target-specific tuning and therefore strongly exercises x86 late optimization quality rather than front-end behavior.
The reported affected machines are AMD Zen2 and Zen5, consistent with a backend cost-model or scheduling mismatch rather than a source-level issue.

The behavior description highlights hot vectorized workloads with repeated scalar-to-vector splats across loops/basic blocks, exactly the scenario where eliminating redundancy can still lose if the shared value becomes too wide or too long-lived.

gcc/haifa-sched.cc.signature: static int model_spill_cost (int cl, int from, int to)
gcc/haifa-sched.cc.summary: Return the cost of increasing the pressure in class CL from FROM to TO. Here we use the very simplistic cost model that every register above sched_class_regs_num[CL] has a spill cost of 1. We could use other measures instead, such as one based on MEMORY_MOVE_COST. However: (1) In order for an instruction to be scheduled, the higher cost would need to be justified in a single saving of that many stalls. This is overly pessimistic, because the benefit of spilling is often to avoid a sequence of several short stalls rather than a single long one. (2) The cost is still arbitrary. Because we are not allocating registers during scheduling, we have no way of knowing for sure how many memory accesses will be required by each spill, where the spills will be placed within the block, or even which block(s) will contain the spills. So a higher cost than 1 is often too conservative in practice, forcing blocks to contain unnecessary stalls instead of spill code. The simple cost below seems to be the best compromise. It reduces the interference with the normal list scheduler, which helps make it more suitable for a default-on option.

Where possible, substitute every register reference in the N_SETS number of SETS in INSN with the canonical register. Register canonicalization propagatest the earliest register (i.e. one that is set before INSN) with the same value. This is a very useful, simple form of CSE, to clean up warts from expanding GIMPLE to RTL. For instance, a CONST for an address is usually expanded multiple times to loads into different registers, thus creating many subexpressions of the form: (set (reg1) (some_const)) (set (mem (... reg1 ...) (thing))) (set (reg2) (some_const)) (set (mem (... reg2 ...) (thing))) After canonicalizing, the code takes the following form: (set (reg1) (some_const)) (set (mem (... reg1 ...) (thing))) (set (reg2) (some_const)) (set (mem (... reg1 ...) (thing))) The set to reg2 is now trivially dead, and the memory reference (or address, or whatever) may be a candidate for further CSEing. In this function, the result of apply_change_group can be ignored; see canon_reg.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool can_split_parallel_of_n_reg_sets (rtx_insn *insn, int n)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return whether INSN, a PARALLEL of N register SETs (and maybe some CLOBBERs), can be split into individual SETs in that order, without changing semantics.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool is_just_move (rtx_insn *x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return whether X is just a single_set, with the source a general_operand.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static int count_auto_inc (rtx, rtx, rtx, rtx, rtx, void *arg)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Callback function to count autoincs.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx_insn * try_combine (rtx_insn *i3, rtx_insn *i2, rtx_insn *i1, rtx_insn *i0, bool *new_direct_jump_p, rtx_insn *last_combined_insn)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Try to combine the insns I0, I1 and I2 into I3. Here I0, I1 and I2 appear earlier than I3. I0 and I1 can be zero; then we combine just I2 into I3, or I1 and I2 into I3. If we are combining more than two insns and the resulting insn is not recognized, try splitting it into two insns. If that happens, I2 and I3 are retained and I1/I0 are pseudo-deleted by turning them into a NOTE. Otherwise, I0, I1 and I2 are pseudo-deleted. Return 0 if the combination does not work. Then nothing is changed. If we did the combination, return the insn at which combine should resume scanning. Set NEW_DIRECT_JUMP_P to true if try_combine creates a new direct jump instruction. LAST_COMBINED_INSN is either I3, or some insn after I3 that has been I3 passed to an earlier try_combine within the same basic block.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void * get_undo_marker (void)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Get a marker for undoing to the current state.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void undo_to_marker (void *marker)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Undo the modifications up to the marker.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void undo_all (void)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Undo all the modifications recorded in undobuf.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void undo_commit (void)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: We've committed to accepting the changes we made. Move all of the undos to the free list.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx * find_split_point (rtx *loc, rtx_insn *insn, bool set_src)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Find the innermost point within the rtx at LOC, possibly LOC itself, where we have an arithmetic expression and return that point. LOC will be inside INSN. try_combine will call this function to see if an insn can be split into two insns.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx subst (rtx x, rtx from, rtx to, bool in_dest, bool in_cond, bool unique_copy)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Throughout X, replace FROM with TO, and return the result. The result is TO if X is FROM; otherwise the result is X, but its contents may have been modified. If they were modified, a record was made in undobuf so that undo_all will (among other things) return X to its original state. If the number of changes necessary is too much to record to undo, the excess changes are not made, so the result is invalid. The changes already made can still be undone. undobuf.num_undo is incremented for such changes, so by testing that the caller can tell whether the result is valid. `n_occurrences' is incremented each time FROM is replaced. IN_DEST is true if we are processing the SET_DEST of a SET. IN_COND is true if we are at the top level of a condition. UNIQUE_COPY is true if each substitution must be unique. We do this by copying if `n_occurrences' is nonzero.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void maybe_swap_commutative_operands (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: If X is a commutative operation whose operands are not in the canonical order, use substitutions to swap them.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx combine_simplify_rtx (rtx x, machine_mode op0_mode, bool in_dest, bool in_cond)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify X, a piece of RTL. We just operate on the expression at the outer level; call `subst' to simplify recursively. Return the new expression. OP0_MODE is the original mode of XEXP (x, 0). IN_DEST is true if we are inside a SET_DEST. IN_COND is true if we are at the top level of a condition.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_if_then_else (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify X, an IF_THEN_ELSE expression. Return the new expression.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_set (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify X, a SET expression. Return the new expression.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_logical (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify, X, and AND, IOR, or XOR operation, and return the simplified result.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx expand_compound_operation (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: We consider ZERO_EXTRACT, SIGN_EXTRACT, and SIGN_EXTEND as "compound operations" because they can be replaced with two more basic operations. ZERO_EXTEND is also considered "compound" because it can be replaced with an AND operation, which is simpler, though only one operation. The function expand_compound_operation is called with an rtx expression and will convert it to the appropriate shifts and AND operations, simplifying at each stage. The function make_compound_operation is called to convert an expression consisting of shifts and ANDs into the equivalent compound expression. It is the inverse of this function, loosely speaking.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static const_rtx expand_field_assignment (const_rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: X is a SET which contains an assignment of one object into a part of another (such as a bit-field assignment, STRICT_LOW_PART, or certain SUBREGS). If possible, convert it into a series of logical operations. We half-heartedly support variable positions, but do not at all support variable lengths.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx make_extraction (machine_mode mode, rtx inner, HOST_WIDE_INT pos, rtx pos_rtx, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT len, bool unsignedp, bool in_dest, bool in_compare)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return an RTX for a reference to LEN bits of INNER. If POS_RTX is nonzero, it is an RTX that represents the (variable) starting position; otherwise, POS is the (constant) starting bit position. Both are counted from the LSB. UNSIGNEDP is true for an unsigned reference and zero for a signed one. IN_DEST is true if this is a reference in the destination of a SET. This is used when a ZERO_ or SIGN_EXTRACT isn't needed. If nonzero, a STRICT_LOW_PART will be used, if zero, ZERO_EXTEND or SIGN_EXTEND will be used. IN_COMPARE is true if we are in a COMPARE. This means that a ZERO_EXTRACT should be built even for bits starting at bit 0. MODE is the desired mode of the result (if IN_DEST == 0). The result is an RTX for the extraction or NULL_RTX if the target can't handle it.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx extract_left_shift (scalar_int_mode mode, rtx x, int count)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: See if X (of mode MODE) contains an ASHIFT of COUNT or more bits that can be commuted with any other operations in X. Return X without that shift if so.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx make_compound_operation_int (scalar_int_mode mode, rtx *x_ptr, enum rtx_code in_code, enum rtx_code *next_code_ptr)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Subroutine of make_compound_operation. *X_PTR is the rtx at the current level of the expression and MODE is its mode. IN_CODE is as for make_compound_operation. *NEXT_CODE_PTR is the value of IN_CODE that should be used when recursing on operands of *X_PTR. There are two possible actions: - Return null. This tells the caller to recurse on *X_PTR with IN_CODE equal to *NEXT_CODE_PTR, after which *X_PTR holds the final value. - Return a new rtx, which the caller returns directly.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: rtx make_compound_operation (rtx x, enum rtx_code in_code)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Look at the expression rooted at X. Look for expressions equivalent to ZERO_EXTRACT, SIGN_EXTRACT, ZERO_EXTEND, SIGN_EXTEND. Form these expressions. Return the new rtx, usually just X. Also, for machines like the VAX that don't have logical shift insns, try to convert logical to arithmetic shift operations in cases where they are equivalent. This undoes the canonicalizations to logical shifts done elsewhere. We try, as much as possible, to re-use rtl expressions to save memory. IN_CODE says what kind of expression we are processing. Normally, it is SET. In a memory address it is MEM. When processing the arguments of a comparison or a COMPARE against zero, it is COMPARE, or EQ if more precisely it is an equality comparison against zero.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static int get_pos_from_mask (unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT m, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT *plen)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Given M see if it is a value that would select a field of bits within an item, but not the entire word. Return -1 if not. Otherwise, return the starting position of the field, where 0 is the low-order bit. PLEN is set to the length of the field.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx canon_reg_for_combine (rtx x, rtx reg)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: If X refers to a register that equals REG in value, replace these references with REG.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx gen_lowpart_or_truncate (machine_mode mode, rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return X converted to MODE. If the value is already truncated to MODE we can just return a subreg even though in the general case we would need an explicit truncation.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx force_to_mode (rtx x, machine_mode mode, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT mask, bool just_select)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: See if X can be simplified knowing that we will only refer to it in MODE and will only refer to those bits that are nonzero in MASK. If other bits are being computed or if masking operations are done that select a superset of the bits in MASK, they can sometimes be ignored. Return a possibly simplified expression, but always convert X to MODE. If X is a CONST_INT, AND the CONST_INT with MASK. If JUST_SELECT is true, don't optimize by noticing that bits in MASK are all off in X. This is used when X will be complemented, by either NOT, NEG, or XOR.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx force_int_to_mode (rtx x, scalar_int_mode mode, scalar_int_mode xmode, scalar_int_mode op_mode, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT mask, bool just_select)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Subroutine of force_to_mode that handles cases in which both X and the result are scalar integers. MODE is the mode of the result, XMODE is the mode of X, and OP_MODE says which of MODE or XMODE is preferred for simplified versions of X. The other arguments are as for force_to_mode.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx if_then_else_cond (rtx x, rtx *ptrue, rtx *pfalse)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return nonzero if X is an expression that has one of two values depending on whether some other value is zero or nonzero. In that case, we return the value that is being tested, *PTRUE is set to the value if the rtx being returned has a nonzero value, and *PFALSE is set to the other alternative. If we return zero, we set *PTRUE and *PFALSE to X.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx known_cond (rtx x, enum rtx_code cond, rtx reg, rtx val)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return the value of expression X given the fact that condition COND is known to be true when applied to REG as its first operand and VAL as its second. X is known to not be shared and so can be modified in place. We only handle the simplest cases, and specifically those cases that arise with IF_THEN_ELSE expressions.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool rtx_equal_for_field_assignment_p (rtx x, rtx y, bool widen_x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: See if X and Y are equal for the purposes of seeing if we can rewrite an assignment as a field assignment.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx make_field_assignment (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: See if X, a SET operation, can be rewritten as a bit-field assignment. Return that assignment if so. We only handle the most common cases.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx apply_distributive_law (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: See if X is of the form (+ (* a c) (* b c)) and convert to (* (+ a b) c) if so.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx distribute_and_simplify_rtx (rtx x, int n)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: See if X is of the form (* (+ A B) C), and if so convert to (+ (* A C) (* B C)) and try to simplify. Most of the time, this results in no change. However, if some of the operands are the same or inverses of each other, simplifications will result. For example, (and (ior A B) (not B)) can occur as the result of expanding a bit field assignment. When we apply the distributive law to this, we get (ior (and (A (not B))) (and (B (not B)))), which then simplifies to (and (A (not B))). Note that no checks happen on the validity of applying the inverse distributive law. This is pointless since we can do it in the few places where this routine is called. N is the index of the term that is decomposed (the arithmetic operation, i.e. (+ A B) in the first example above). !N is the index of the term that is distributed, i.e. of C in the first example above.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_and_const_int_1 (scalar_int_mode mode, rtx varop, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT constop)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify a logical `and' of VAROP with the constant CONSTOP, to be done in MODE. Return an equivalent form, if different from (and VAROP (const_int CONSTOP)). Otherwise, return NULL_RTX.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_and_const_int (rtx x, scalar_int_mode mode, rtx varop, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT constop)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: We have X, a logical `and' of VAROP with the constant CONSTOP, to be done in MODE. Return an equivalent form, if different from X. Otherwise, return X. If X is zero, we are to always construct the equivalent form.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx reg_nonzero_bits_for_combine (const_rtx x, scalar_int_mode xmode, scalar_int_mode mode, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT *nonzero)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Given a REG X of mode XMODE, compute which bits in X can be nonzero. We don't care about bits outside of those defined in MODE. We DO care about all the bits in MODE, even if XMODE is smaller than MODE. For most X this is simply GET_MODE_MASK (GET_MODE (MODE)), but if X is a shift, AND, or zero_extract, we can do better.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx reg_num_sign_bit_copies_for_combine (const_rtx x, scalar_int_mode xmode, scalar_int_mode mode, unsigned int *result)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Given a reg X of mode XMODE, return the number of bits at the high-order end of X that are known to be equal to the sign bit. X will be used in mode MODE; the returned value will always be between 1 and the number of bits in MODE.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: unsigned int extended_count (const_rtx x, machine_mode mode, bool unsignedp)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return the number of "extended" bits there are in X, when interpreted as a quantity in MODE whose signedness is indicated by UNSIGNEDP. For unsigned quantities, this is the number of high-order zero bits. For signed quantities, this is the number of copies of the sign bit minus 1. In both case, this function returns the number of "spare" bits. For example, if two quantities for which this function returns at least 1 are added, the addition is known not to overflow. This function will always return 0 unless called during combine, which implies that it must be called from a define_split.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool merge_outer_ops (enum rtx_code *pop0, HOST_WIDE_INT *pconst0, enum rtx_code op1, HOST_WIDE_INT const1, machine_mode mode, bool *pcomp_p)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: This function is called from `simplify_shift_const' to merge two outer operations. Specifically, we have already found that we need to perform operation *POP0 with constant *PCONST0 at the outermost position. We would now like to also perform OP1 with constant CONST1 (with *POP0 being done last). Return true if we can do the operation and update *POP0 and *PCONST0 with the resulting operation. *PCOMP_P is set to true if we would need to complement the innermost operand, otherwise it is unchanged. MODE is the mode in which the operation will be done. No bits outside the width of this mode matter. It is assumed that the width of this mode is smaller than or equal to HOST_BITS_PER_WIDE_INT. If *POP0 or OP1 are UNKNOWN, it means no operation is required. Only NEG, PLUS, IOR, XOR, and AND are supported. We may set *POP0 to SET if the proper result is simply *PCONST0. If the resulting operation cannot be expressed as one operation, we return false and do not change *POP0, *PCONST0, and *PCOMP_P.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static scalar_int_mode try_widen_shift_mode (enum rtx_code code, rtx op, int count, scalar_int_mode orig_mode, scalar_int_mode mode, enum rtx_code outer_code, HOST_WIDE_INT outer_const)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: A helper to simplify_shift_const_1 to determine the mode we can perform the shift in. The original shift operation CODE is performed on OP in ORIG_MODE. Return the wider mode MODE if we can perform the operation in that mode. Return ORIG_MODE otherwise. We can also assume that the result of the shift is subject to operation OUTER_CODE with operand OUTER_CONST.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_shift_const_1 (enum rtx_code code, machine_mode result_mode, rtx varop, int orig_count)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify a shift of VAROP by ORIG_COUNT bits. CODE says what kind of shift. The result of the shift is RESULT_MODE. Return NULL_RTX if we cannot simplify it. Otherwise, return a simplified value. The shift is normally computed in the widest mode we find in VAROP, as long as it isn't a different number of words than RESULT_MODE. Exceptions are ASHIFTRT and ROTATE, which are always done in their original mode.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_shift_const (rtx x, enum rtx_code code, machine_mode result_mode, rtx varop, int count)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify a shift of VAROP by COUNT bits. CODE says what kind of shift. The result of the shift is RESULT_MODE. If we cannot simplify it, return X or, if it is NULL, synthesize the expression with simplify_gen_binary. Otherwise, return a simplified value. The shift is normally computed in the widest mode we find in VAROP, as long as it isn't a different number of words than RESULT_MODE. Exceptions are ASHIFTRT and ROTATE, which are always done in their original mode.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static int recog_for_combine_1 (rtx *pnewpat, rtx_insn *insn, rtx *pnotes, unsigned old_nregs, unsigned new_nregs)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: A subroutine of recog_for_combine. See there for arguments and return value.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool change_zero_ext (rtx pat)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Change every ZERO_EXTRACT and ZERO_EXTEND of a SUBREG that can be expressed as an AND and maybe an LSHIFTRT, to that formulation. Return whether anything was so changed.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static int recog_for_combine (rtx *pnewpat, rtx_insn *insn, rtx *pnotes, unsigned int old_nregs, unsigned int new_nregs)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Like recog, but we receive the address of a pointer to a new pattern. We try to match the rtx that the pointer points to. If that fails, we may try to modify or replace the pattern, storing the replacement into the same pointer object. Modifications include deletion or addition of CLOBBERs. If the instruction will still not match, we change ZERO_EXTEND and ZERO_EXTRACT to the equivalent AND and perhaps LSHIFTRT patterns, and try with that (and undo if that fails). PNOTES is a pointer to a location where any REG_UNUSED notes added for the CLOBBERs are placed. If OLD_NREGS != NEW_NREGS, then PNOTES also includes REG_DEAD notes added. The value is the final insn code from the pattern ultimately matched, or -1.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx gen_lowpart_for_combine (machine_mode omode, rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Like gen_lowpart_general but for use by combine. In combine it is not possible to create any new pseudoregs. However, it is safe to create invalid memory addresses, because combine will try to recognize them and all they will do is make the combine attempt fail. If for some reason this cannot do its job, an rtx (clobber (const_int 0)) is returned. An insn containing that will not be recognized.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx gen_lowpart_for_combine_no_emit (machine_mode omode, rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Like gen_lowpart_for_combine but returns NULL_RTX for an error instead of CLOBBER. Note no_emit is not called directly from combine but rather from simplify_rtx and is expecting a NULL on failure rather than a CLOBBER.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static enum rtx_code simplify_compare_const (enum rtx_code code, machine_mode mode, rtx *pop0, rtx *pop1)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Try to simplify a comparison between OP0 and a constant OP1, where CODE is the comparison code that will be tested, into a (CODE OP0 const0_rtx) form. The result is a possibly different comparison code to use. POP0 and *POP1 may be updated.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static enum rtx_code simplify_comparison (enum rtx_code code, rtx *pop0, rtx *pop1)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify a comparison between *POP0 and *POP1 where CODE is the comparison code that will be tested. The result is a possibly different comparison code to use. *POP0 and POP1 may be updated. It is possible that we might detect that a comparison is either always true or always false. However, we do not perform general constant folding in combine, so this knowledge isn't useful. Such tautologies should have been detected earlier. Hence we ignore all such cases.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static int count_rtxs (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Utility function for record_value_for_reg. Count number of rtxs in X.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void update_table_tick (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Utility function for following routine. Called when X is part of a value being stored into last_set_value. Sets last_set_table_tick for each register mentioned. Similar to mention_regs in cse.cc

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void record_value_for_reg (rtx reg, rtx_insn *insn, rtx value)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Record that REG is set to VALUE in insn INSN. If VALUE is zero, we are saying that the register is clobbered and we no longer know its value. If INSN is zero, don't update reg_stat[].last_set; this is only permitted with VALUE also zero and is used to invalidate the register.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void record_dead_and_set_regs_1 (rtx dest, const_rtx setter, void *data)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Called via note_stores from record_dead_and_set_regs to handle one SET or CLOBBER in an insn. DATA is the instruction in which the set is occurring.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void record_dead_and_set_regs (rtx_insn *insn)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Update the records of when each REG was most recently set or killed for the things done by INSN. This is the last thing done in processing INSN in the combiner loop. We update reg_stat[], in particular fields last_set, last_set_value, last_set_mode, last_set_nonzero_bits, last_set_sign_bit_copies, last_death, and also the similar information mem_last_set (which insn most recently modified memory) and last_call_luid (which insn was the most recent subroutine call).

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void record_promoted_value (rtx_insn *insn, rtx subreg)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: If a SUBREG has the promoted bit set, it is in fact a property of the register present in the SUBREG, so for each such SUBREG go back and adjust nonzero and sign bit information of the registers that are known to have some zero/sign bits set. This is needed because when combine blows the SUBREGs away, the information on zero/sign bits is lost and further combines can be missed because of that.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool reg_truncated_to_mode (machine_mode mode, const_rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Check if X, a register, is known to contain a value already truncated to MODE. In this case we can use a subreg to refer to the truncated value even though in the generic case we would need an explicit truncation.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool record_truncated_value (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: If X is a hard reg or a subreg record the mode that the register is accessed in. For non-TARGET_TRULY_NOOP_TRUNCATION targets we might be able to turn a truncate into a subreg using this information. Return true if traversing X is complete.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void record_truncated_values (rtx *loc, void *data ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Callback for note_uses. Find hardregs and subregs of pseudos and the modes they are used in. This can help truning TRUNCATEs into SUBREGs.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void check_promoted_subreg (rtx_insn *insn, rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Scan X for promoted SUBREGs. For each one found, note what it implies to the registers used in it.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool get_last_value_validate (rtx *loc, rtx_insn *insn, int tick, bool replace)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Verify that all the registers and memory references mentioned in *LOC are still valid. *LOC was part of a value set in INSN when label_tick was equal to TICK. Return false if some are not. If REPLACE is true, replace the invalid references with (clobber (const_int 0)) and return true. This replacement is useful because we often can get useful information about the form of a value (e.g., if it was produced by a shift that always produces -1 or 0) even though we don't know exactly what registers it was produced from.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx get_last_value (const_rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Get the last value assigned to X, if known. Some registers in the value may be replaced with (clobber (const_int 0)) if their value is known longer known reliably.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void reg_dead_at_p_1 (rtx dest, const_rtx x, void *data ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Function called via note_stores from reg_dead_at_p. If DEST is within [reg_dead_regno, reg_dead_endregno), set reg_dead_flag to 1 if X is a CLOBBER and to -1 it is a SET.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool reg_dead_at_p (rtx reg, rtx_insn *insn)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return true if REG is known to be dead at INSN. We scan backwards from INSN. If we hit a REG_DEAD note or a CLOBBER referencing REG, it is dead. If we hit a SET referencing REG, it is live. Otherwise, see if it is live or dead at the start of the basic block we are in. Hard regs marked as being live in NEWPAT_USED_REGS must be assumed to be always live.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void mark_used_regs_combine (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Note hard registers in X that are used.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: rtx remove_death (unsigned int regno, rtx_insn *insn)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Remove register number REGNO from the dead registers list of INSN. Return the note used to record the death, if there was one.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void move_deaths (rtx x, rtx maybe_kill_insn, int from_luid, rtx_insn *to_insn, rtx *pnotes)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: For each register (hardware or pseudo) used within expression X, if its death is in an instruction with luid between FROM_LUID (inclusive) and TO_INSN (exclusive), put a REG_DEAD note for that register in the list headed by PNOTES. That said, don't move registers killed by maybe_kill_insn. This is done when X is being merged by combination into TO_INSN. These notes will then be distributed as needed.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool reg_bitfield_target_p (rtx x, rtx body)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return true if X is the target of a bit-field assignment in BODY, the pattern of an insn. X must be a REG.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void distribute_notes (rtx notes, rtx_insn *from_insn, rtx_insn *i3, rtx_insn *i2, rtx elim_i2, rtx elim_i1, rtx elim_i0)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Given a chain of REG_NOTES originally from FROM_INSN, try to place them as appropriate. I3 and I2 are the insns resulting from the combination insns including FROM (I2 may be zero). ELIM_I2 and ELIM_I1 are either zero or registers that we know will not need REG_DEAD notes because they are being substituted for. This saves searching in the most common cases. Each note in the list is either ignored or placed on some insns, depending on the type of note.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void distribute_links (struct insn_link *links, rtx_insn *start, int limit)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Similarly to above, distribute the LOG_LINKS that used to be present on I3, I2, and I1 to new locations. This is also called to add a link pointing at I3 when I3's destination is changed. If START is nonnull and an insn, we know that the next location for each link is no earlier than START. LIMIT is the maximum number of nondebug instructions that can be scanned when looking for the next use of a definition.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool unmentioned_reg_p (rtx equiv, rtx expr)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Check for any register or memory mentioned in EQUIV that is not mentioned in EXPR. This is used to restrict EQUIV to "specializations" of EXPR where some registers may have been replaced by constants.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void make_more_copies (void)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Make pseudo-to-pseudo copies after every hard-reg-to-pseudo-copy, because the reg-to-reg copy can usefully combine with later instructions, but we do not want to combine the hard reg into later instructions, for that restricts register allocation.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void rest_of_handle_combine (void)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Try combining insns through substitution.

related_methods.reason: The regression is about the pass choosing a single 'widest' broadcast for reuse. This method determines the natural machine mode for vector types and explicitly deals with cases where only some vector ISA extensions are enabled, making it the most relevant place for width-selection decisions that could inflate broadcasts and hurt Zen2/Zen5 performance.

The bad commit extends redundant-vector removal for broadcasts from constants, and this method selects the opcode used to materialize supported SSE/AVX vector constants. If widened constant broadcasts are being emitted in a suboptimal form, this opcode-selection logic is a likely contributor to the observed backend performance regression.

This is the central routine that walks each basic block and updates allocno live ranges, hard-register conflicts, intersected calls, and register-pressure information. The reported regression is most plausibly caused by widened/hoisted broadcasts creating longer live ranges across blocks, and this method is where those cross-BB liveness and pressure effects are computed, making it the most likely place for a profitability-distorting bug to surface.

The bug report points to a performance regression driven by increased vector live ranges and register pressure on Zen2/Zen5. This helper directly updates excess-pressure metrics for an allocno, so if widened broadcasts are causing pressure but that cost is being tracked inaccurately, this method could let IRA underestimate the harm and choose worse allocation outcomes.

This is the main driver that derives register-class and memory costs and chooses preferred/alternative classes for pseudos. A regression caused by hoisted widest-vector broadcasts can show up here as bad cost modeling for long-lived wide vector pseudos, leading IRA to prefer classes or placements that increase spills and register pressure on Zen2/Zen5.

This routine records operand costs for hard-register classes across insns and alternatives, so it is a likely place where the cost impact of wider broadcasted vectors is mis-estimated. If the extended broadcast optimization changes operand modes and constraints, weak accounting here could make redundant-vector removal look profitable while steering allocation toward more expensive wide-register usage.

This hook explicitly adjusts priorities to shorten or lengthen register lifetimes. The regression scenario involves hoisted, wider vector broadcasts that can extend live ranges and increase pressure, so a bad priority tweak here could easily make scheduling worse instead of better.

This function decides whether an instruction hurts or helps register pressure. If the new vector-broadcast patterns are underestimated here, the scheduler may choose an order that looks cheap in the model but creates longer-lived wide vectors and worse code on Zen2/Zen5.

The regressing x86 change explicitly hoists broadcasts to the nearest common dominator of multiple use blocks. This helper computes exactly that placement point for a set of blocks, so any flaw in how it selects or reduces the set can directly cause overly high hoisting, longer vector live ranges, and the observed performance slowdown.

This is the core pairwise primitive behind common-dominator placement. If it returns a dominator that is correct structurally but higher than profitability expects, the remove_redundant_vector pass can materialize broadcasts too early, increasing register pressure across hot paths on Zen2/Zen5.

This routine decides which equivalent RTX is more desirable. A performance-only regression caused by replacing local/narrow vector broadcasts with a shared wider value matches a bad profitability choice here: if the comparison prefers a seemingly cheaper expression without accounting for longer live ranges, wider modes, or target-specific register-pressure costs, CSE can reinforce the same kind of slowdown seen in the bug report.

This function substitutes register references with the canonical equivalent register, explicitly favoring the earliest available producer. That kind of canonicalization can lengthen the lifetime of a vector value across more instructions and blocks, which is a strong fit for the observed AMD slowdown where hoisted/shared broadcasts become long-lived and hurt allocation or scheduling.

This is the clearest profitability gate in `combine.cc`: it decides whether replacement patterns are more expensive than the original sequence. The reported bug is a pure performance regression caused by transformations that look redundant-removing in RTL terms but become slower on Zen2/Zen5 because of wider broadcasts, longer live ranges, and register pressure. If `combine` accepts such reshaped vector patterns with an insufficient target-cost model, this method is a prime place for the mistake.

`try_combine` is the main transformation engine that substitutes earlier defs into later insns, potentially changing where values are materialized and how wide they are. That is very similar to the failure mode described in the bug report: replacing multiple local broadcasts with one shared wider value can hurt scheduling and RA. Any combine-time rewrite of vector splats, subregs, or mode changes that amplifies the new x86 pass would most likely flow through this method.

reviewed_methods.summary: Find the nearest common dominator for the basic blocks in BLOCKS, using dominance direction DIR.
reviewed_methods.reason: The bad commit explicitly hoists a single widest broadcast to the nearest common dominator of all uses, so this helper sits directly on the placement path. The most likely issue is still profitability in the caller rather than incorrect dominance computation, but among the listed methods this is one of the closest to the new regressing behavior.

Even so, the routine is a generic and well-established dominator query; a wrong policy in how the pass uses the result is more likely than a bug here.

reviewed_methods.reason: Bad register-class cost modeling can turn widened broadcasts into spills and poor allocation, which matches the slowdown symptoms. reviewed_methods.reason: This code is where longer vector live ranges and pressure become visible to IRA, so it is relevant to the observed slowdown. Still, the regression is bisected to a specific x86 optimization pass change, making IRA liveness more likely a victim of worse input than the root cause.

reviewed_methods.signature: static rtx_insn * try_combine (rtx_insn *i3, rtx_insn *i2, rtx_insn *i1, rtx_insn *i0, bool *new_direct_jump_p, rtx_insn *last_combined_insn)
reviewed_methods.summary: Try to combine the insns I0, I1 and I2 into I3. Here I0, I1 and I2 appear earlier than I3. I0 and I1 can be zero; then we combine just I2 into I3, or I1 and I2 into I3. If we are combining more than two insns and the resulting insn is not recognized, try splitting it into two insns. If that happens, I2 and I3 are retained and I1/I0 are pseudo-deleted by turning them into a NOTE. Otherwise, I0, I1 and I2 are pseudo-deleted. Return 0 if the combination does not work. Then nothing is changed. If we did the combination, return the insn at which combine should resume scanning. Set NEW_DIRECT_JUMP_P to true if try_combine creates a new direct jump instruction. LAST_COMBINED_INSN is either I3, or some insn after I3 that has been I3 passed to an earlier try_combine within the same basic block.
reviewed_methods.reason: `try_combine` is the main RTL combiner transformation engine and could interact badly with widened vector splats or reuse of earlier values, so it is a credible secondary suspect. Still, the bug is bisected to a specific x86 pass extension whose documented behavior directly matches the regression mechanism: creating one shared widest broadcast and hoisting it to a common dominator or definition site. Unless the x86 pass is merely exposing an older combine weakness, the best fix location is more likely in that pass's profitability or placement logic than in this broad generic combiner routine.

reviewed_methods.signature: static void record_reg_classes (int n_alts, int n_ops, rtx *ops, machine_mode *modes, const char **constraints, rtx_insn *insn, enum reg_class *pref)
reviewed_methods.summary: Record the cost of using memory or hard registers of various classes for the operands in INSN. N_ALTS is the number of alternatives. N_OPS is the number of operands. OPS is an array of the operands. MODES are the modes of the operands, in case any are VOIDmode. CONSTRAINTS are the constraints to use for the operands. This array is modified by this procedure. This procedure works alternative by alternative. For each alternative we assume that we will be able to allocate all allocnos to their ideal register class and calculate the cost of using that alternative. Then we compute, for each operand that is a pseudo-register, the cost of having the allocno allocated to each register class and using it in that alternative. To this cost is added the cost of the alternative. The cost of each class for this insn is its lowest cost among all the alternatives.
reviewed_methods.reason: This routine models operand/class costs and could misprice wider vector uses, but it does not implement the new dominator-based broadcast sharing. It is a believable contributor to backend sensitivity, not the strongest location to fix the regression-triggering behavior.

reviewed_methods.summary: Update ALLOCNO_EXCESS_PRESSURE_POINTS_NUM for the allocno associated with object OBJ.
reviewed_methods.reason: Pressure accounting could amplify the damage from hoisted wide broadcasts, but this helper is a narrow metric update and not the place where the harmful transformation is chosen. It is plausible only if pressure is being systematically under-modeled for the new pattern.

reviewed_methods.signature: static bool combine_validate_cost (rtx_insn *i0, rtx_insn *i1, rtx_insn *i2, rtx_insn *i3, rtx newpat, rtx newi2pat, rtx newotherpat)
reviewed_methods.summary: Subroutine of try_combine. Determine whether the replacement patterns NEWPAT, NEWI2PAT and NEWOTHERPAT are more expensive according to insn_cost than the original sequence I0, I1, I2, I3 and undobuf.other_insn. Note that I0, I1 and/or NEWI2PAT may be NULL_RTX. Similarly, NEWOTHERPAT and undobuf.other_insn may also both be NULL_RTX. Return false if the cost of all the instructions can be estimated and the replacements are more expensive than the original sequence.
reviewed_methods.reason: This is a genuine profitability gate and therefore more relevant than generic CSE helpers for a performance-only regression. However, it operates on combine candidates after patterns have already been formed, using general insn cost estimates rather than pass-specific logic about hoisting scalar-to-vector broadcasts, choosing the widest mode, or limiting dominance span. Since the regression is explicitly introduced by a commit in the x86 remove_redundant_vector pass, this method is more likely to expose insufficient downstream costing than to be the primary place to fix the bug.

reviewed_methods.signature: static machine_mode type_natural_mode (const_tree type, const CUMULATIVE_ARGS *cum, bool in_return)
reviewed_methods.summary: Return the "natural" mode for TYPE. In most cases, this is just TYPE_MODE. But in the case of vector types, it is some vector mode. When we have only some of our vector isa extensions enabled, then there are some modes for which vector_mode_supported_p is false. For these modes, the generic vector support in gcc will choose some non-vector mode in order to implement the type. By computing the natural mode, we'll select the proper ABI location for the operand and not depend on whatever the middle-end decides to do with these vector types. The midde-end can't deal with the vector types > 16 bytes. In this case, we return the original mode and warn ABI change if CUM isn't NULL. If INT_RETURN is true, warn ABI change if the vector mode isn't available for function return value.
reviewed_methods.reason: Width selection is part of the regression story, but this routine is mainly ABI/natural-mode selection for vector types, not the profitability logic of the new remove_redundant_vector transformation. It is only an indirect contributor unless the pass is wrongly asking for an unnecessarily wide mode through this helper.

reviewed_methods.summary: Return (in order): - positive if INSN adversely affects the pressure on one register class - negative if INSN reduces the pressure on one register class - 0 if INSN doesn't affect the pressure on any register class.
reviewed_methods.reason: Scheduler pressure classification could worsen the effect of long-lived wide vectors, but this is downstream fallout. Nothing in the bug report suggests a scheduler regression started independently; the triggering change is earlier and more directly about code motion of broadcasts.

reviewed_methods.summary: Return the opcode of the special instruction to be used to load the constant operands[1] into operands[0].
reviewed_methods.reason: The bug is a large performance regression introduced by broadcast-hoisting/reuse, not obviously by choosing a wrong constant-load opcode. This function affects instruction form for constants, but it does not decide whether to hoist, merge, or widen broadcasts across blocks, so it is a weak primary fix location.

reviewed_methods.summary: Where possible, substitute every register reference in the N_SETS number of SETS in INSN with the canonical register. Register canonicalization propagatest the earliest register (i.e. one that is set before INSN) with the same value. This is a very useful, simple form of CSE, to clean up warts from expanding GIMPLE to RTL. For instance, a CONST for an address is usually expanded multiple times to loads into different registers, thus creating many subexpressions of the form: (set (reg1) (some_const)) (set (mem (... reg1 ...) (thing))) (set (reg2) (some_const)) (set (mem (... reg2 ...) (thing))) After canonicalizing, the code takes the following form: (set (reg1) (some_const)) (set (mem (... reg1 ...) (thing))) (set (reg2) (some_const)) (set (mem (... reg1 ...) (thing))) The set to reg2 is now trivially dead, and the memory reference (or address, or whatever) may be a candidate for further CSEing. In this function, the result of apply_change_group can be ignored; see canon_reg.
reviewed_methods.reason: `canonicalize_insn` can lengthen lifetimes by replacing uses with an earlier canonical register, which superficially resembles the slowdown mechanism. But it is part of generic RTL CSE cleanup within extended basic blocks, whereas the bug report points to a newly extended x86 pass that merges broadcasts across blocks via nearest-common-dominator placement and widest-mode selection. That makes this method a plausible amplifier of bad code shape, but not the most likely root fix location.

reviewed_methods.signature: static int preferable (int cost_a, int regcost_a, int cost_b, int regcost_b)
reviewed_methods.summary: Return a negative value if an rtx A, whose costs are given by COST_A and REGCOST_A, is more desirable than an rtx B. Return a positive value if A is less desirable, or 0 if the two are equally good.
reviewed_methods.reason: This function is a generic local CSE tie-breaker that compares operation cost and register-pressure cost when choosing among already-equivalent RTXes. The reported regression is tightly bisected to the x86 remove_redundant_vector extension, especially its new dominator-based hoisting and widest-broadcast reuse logic. While `preferable` does mention lifetime and register pressure, it is not specific to vector broadcast placement, width inflation, or the x86 target pass named in the regression, so it is only a weak indirect candidate.
